data.raw_text:
So…

I have been watching (with a mix of fascination and unease) a series of YouTube videos that have become something of a genre in contemporary Filipino media: the celebrity van tour, the house tour, the curated glimpse into a life of polished interiors, bespoke furniture, and imported finishes.

And yet, whenever I watch them, there is a stubborn image in my mind that I cannot shake.

I see the gleaming marble countertops and the neatly arranged designer closets, yes… but I also see the gates opening to the same chaotic streets we all share. The house, no matter how immaculate, stands within a horizon tangled with electrical wires, ringed by cracked pavements, shadowed by billboards peeling under the sun.

I cannot separate the interior from the exterior. They are two halves of the same picture. The backdrop refuses to fade.

The same happens with those custom-built luxury vans: plush leather seats, hidden compartments, ambient lighting.

But in my mind’s eye, I cannot help but picture them wedged in the same EDSA traffic, crawling past crumbling sidewalks and haphazard signage, flanked by rusted jeepneys and exhaust fumes.

Even more striking is when their owners step out: the designer sunglasses, the monogrammed handbags, the limited-edition sneakers, the immaculate tailoring.

Every detail is calculated for luxury.

And yet, the frame around them is still the same — potholes, tangled wires, uneven concrete, the harsh smell of animal excrement.

The contrast is not glamorous to me. It collapses into a single image where the ugliness of the environment bleeds into the beauty of the attire.

What strikes me is not merely the display of affluence (which is, after all, the implicit purpose of such spectacles) but the cognitive and aesthetic dissonance they seem to demand.

These immaculate private spaces exist within, and are materially dependent upon, an urban environment whose public face is inescapably dilapidated and (dare I say) ugly.

But in these videos, there is no acknowledgment of this backdrop. It simply disappears from the frame, as though irrelevant to the subject’s self-understanding.

This is not, I think, solely the prerogative of celebrities or the affluent. I have seen the same disposition among acquaintances who, regardless of their means, carry themselves as though their self-image were entirely insulated from the conditions around them. The street could be crumbling, the air heavy with exhaust, but they remain untouched (or at least untroubled) by the contrast. Their sense of self seems anchored not in the shared reality of the environment, but in a private, portable world they construct around themselves through dress, grooming, and the careful curation of possessions.

I cannot inhabit that posture. My sense of self is porous to my surroundings. The state of the street seeps into my own self-perception. To step into urban blight while attempting to look immaculate feels, to me, like a contradiction that cannot be resolved.

This is not a question of fashion or personal taste, but of the ontology of the self: I experience myself as inseparable from the conditions I share with others. The public realm is part of my personal reality.

Marx wrote of alienation not only in terms of labor but in terms of life itself: the estrangement of human beings from the conditions of their own existence, and from one another, under a system that privatizes both wealth and dignity. The ability to maintain one’s image while remaining indifferent to the degradation of shared space is, in a sense, a form of aesthetic alienation. It is the detachment of one’s self-worth from the collective reality, the narrowing of one’s “real” environment to that which is privately owned and controlled.

I wonder if there will be another fire fight on the polo field only this time leaving the field littered with dead PLA troops instead?
